doc.title: Bobby Johnson Jr. interviewed by Monk Rowe, Ellenville, New York, June 23, 1998

title: Singing on the radio the night World War II ended
summary: At the Hotel Lincoln with Hawkins, an announcer interrupted to say the war had ended; he wonders if a recording survives.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: I understand you were singing on the radio when a very important announcement was made in 1945?

Well I swore I’d never talk about it because people, you know people may say that — right now — I think about it, the night, and I could tell you, the night that World War II ended. It was ABC. And there was a lot of things happening. We were in the Hotel Lincoln. As you know, the Hotel Lincoln was the only one in New York that used black bands. Our band and Count Basie. As a matter of fact our band and Count Basie, maybe Lionel Hampton, were the only bands that played the big hotels. The Hotel Lincoln, when I was with Erskine we were the only bands that played the Hotel Aster. We were the only black band that played the 400 Club on Broadway, for some reason, I don’t know. But we knew that there was something happening and we were in a rush to get back to the hotel because we got back and we took our seats and the song that I sang — I wasn’t really the boy singer with Erskine, but I did my parts you know. And we were singing [sings] “Saturday night is the loneliest night in the week.” And all of a sudden a guy came out and waved his hand and he said, “Ladies and Gentlemen, World War II has ended.”

That hit us. And you know what day — that is what changed the world. And they just cut me out maybe, and they kept singing. But I tried to find out whether the Smithsonian, or maybe, I’ve looked for it in my own way to try to find out exactly — I know during those days we had what we called V-disks, large records like that that could take off two or three different, and people, you had to handle them with care because they would break
just like regular. And I know it was taken off on a V-disk but I don’t think it was taken off like anything —
Like the radio wire or something?

Yeah like the radio wire. I don’t think it was taken off like that. But I think maybe during those days the Smithsonian Institute would have a lot of things. I’ve tried to look for it, and I’ve said, any many people oh come on, you’ll never hear it. But someone had to be — this was at the Blue Room at the Hotel Lincoln, the night World War II was over, and man, you’ve never seen people — you’ve seen that famous photo of the sailor kissing the girl and all of that kind of stuff was happening. And then sadly to say, that was the beginning of the end of the big band era. That was the beginning of the end of the era because when television came in the early ‘50’s, that was the end of it. But I still do all right, I can’t kick. I have a gig tomorrow night.
